es.summary: Daño súbito al cerebro causado por golpe, impacto o penetración del cráneo, que puede ser leve (conmoción) o grave con riesgo de coma y muerte.
key_points: Clasificación según gravedad: leve, moderada, grave
Control de la presión intracraneal es prioridad
Intervenciones tempranas reducen morbilidad y mortalidad

pathophysiology: Impacto mecánico produce contusión y/o laceración cerebral
Daño primario genera edema, hemorragia y ruptura de la barrera hematoencefálica
Respuesta inflamatoria produce edema secundario y aumento de la presión intracraneal (PIC)
Disminución del flujo cerebral lleva a hipoxia y necrosis neuronal
signs_symptoms: Pérdida de conciencia o amnesia post‑traumática
Vómitos, cefalea intensa y visión borrosa
Alteraciones del nivel de conciencia (Escala de Glasgow)
diagnostics: TC de cráneo: hemorragia subdural, contusión, fractura
ICP monitor: presión >20 mm Hg indica hipertensión intracraneal
CBC, glucosa, electrolitos (Na⁺, K⁺ en mEq/L) para detectar desequilibrios
treatment: Elevación de la cabecera 30° y control de la PIC (mannitol, solución salina hipertónica)
Ventilación mecánica con control de PaCO₂ (35‑40 mm Hg)
complications: Síndrome de apnea central, trombosis venosa profunda
Déficits cognitivos y trastornos del sueño
nursing_care: Evaluar nivel de conciencia cada hora (Escala de Glasgow)
Monitorear PIC, MAP y signos de hipertensión intracraneal (pupilas, vómitos)
Mantener hidratación y equilibrio electrolítico; registrar ingesta y salida
Posicionar al paciente en decúbito supino con cabeza neutra; evitar estímulos dolorosos
patient_teaching: Explicar la importancia de evitar esfuerzos que aumenten la PIC

outcomes: Mantener integridad cutánea sin lesiones durante la hospitalización
No presentar caídas ni traumatismos adicionales

interventions.action: Colocar al paciente en cama con barandillas elevadas y supervisión constante
interventions.rationale: Previene caídas y protege la cabeza de nuevos traumatismos

interventions.action: Evaluar nivel de conciencia y pupilas cada hora
Mantener el entorno libre de obstáculos y con iluminación adecuada
interventions.rationale: Reduce riesgo de tropiezos y caídas

interventions.action: Aplicar dispositivos de inmovilización según indicación médica
interventions.rationale: Evita movimientos bruscos que puedan aumentar la presión intracraneal

evidenced_by: cansancio al realizar actividades de la vida diaria
aumento de la presión arterial durante actividad
outcomes: Participar en actividades de ADL con ayuda mínima sin aumento de la PIC
Mantener nivel de actividad tolerado sin signos de deterioro neurológico

interventions.action: Planificar períodos de reposo cada 30‑45 min de actividad ligera
interventions.rationale: Previene el agotamiento y controla la presión intracraneal

interventions.action: Monitorizar signos vitales y nivel de conciencia antes y después de la actividad
Enseñar técnicas de respiración profunda y relajación
interventions.rationale: Reduce la respuesta simpática y la presión arterial

interventions.action: Coordinar con fisioterapia para ejercicios de bajo impacto y progresivos
interventions.rationale: Mejora la tolerancia física sin sobrecargar el cerebro

interventions.action: Registrar nivel de fatiga usando escala de Borg y ajustar actividades
interventions.rationale: Permite individualizar el plan de cuidados

en.summary: Sudden damage to the brain caused by a blow, impact, or penetration of the skull, which can be mild (concussion) or severe with risk of coma and death.
key_points: Classification by severity: mild, moderate, severe
Intracranial pressure control is a priority
Early interventions reduce morbidity and mortality

pathophysiology: Mechanical impact produces contusion and/or cerebral laceration
Primary injury generates edema, hemorrhage, and blood‑brain barrier rupture
Inflammatory response produces secondary edema and increased intracranial pressure (ICP)
Reduced cerebral blood flow leads to hypoxia and neuronal necrosis
signs_symptoms: Loss of consciousness or post‑traumatic amnesia
Altered level of consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale)
diagnostics: Head CT: subdural hemorrhage, contusion, fracture
ICP monitor: pressure >20 mm Hg indicates intracranial hypertension
CBC, glucose, electrolytes (Na⁺, K⁺ in mEq/L) to detect imbalances
treatment: Head elevation 30° and ICP control (mannitol, hypertonic saline)
Mechanical ventilation with PaCO₂ control (35‑40 mm Hg)
complications: Central apnea syndrome, deep vein thrombosis
nursing_care: Assess level of consciousness hourly (Glasgow Coma Scale)
Monitor ICP, MAP, and signs of intracranial hypertension (pupils, vomiting)
Maintain hydration and electrolyte balance; record intake and output
Position patient supine with neutral head; avoid painful stimuli
patient_teaching: Explain the importance of avoiding activities that increase ICP

outcomes: Maintain skin integrity without lesions during hospitalization

interventions.action: Place patient in bed with raised rails and constant supervision
interventions.rationale: Prevents falls and protects the head from new trauma

interventions.action: Assess level of consciousness and pupils hourly
Keep environment free of obstacles and with adequate lighting
interventions.rationale: Reduces risk of tripping and falls

interventions.action: Apply immobilization devices as ordered by the physician
interventions.rationale: Prevents sudden movements that could increase intracranial pressure

evidenced_by: tiredness during activities of daily living
outcomes: Participate in ADL activities with minimal assistance without ICP increase
Maintain tolerated activity level without signs of neurological decline

interventions.action: Plan rest periods every 30‑45 min of light activity
interventions.rationale: Prevents exhaustion and controls intracranial pressure

interventions.action: Monitor vital signs and level of consciousness before and after activity
Teach deep breathing and relaxation techniques
interventions.rationale: Reduces sympathetic response and blood pressure

interventions.action: Coordinate with physical therapy for low‑impact, progressive exercises
interventions.rationale: Improves physical tolerance without overloading the brain

interventions.action: Record fatigue level using the Borg scale and adjust activities

summary.0.quote: More severe TBI can lead to serious physical and psychological symptoms, coma , and even death.

key_points.0.quote: Symptoms of a TBI can be mild, moderate, or severe.

key_points.1.quote: A TBI can also happen when an object penetrates the skull.

sections.risk_factors.0.quote: This is the most common cause in adults age 65 and older.

sections.risk_factors.1.quote: Motor vehicle crashes. This is the most common cause in young adults.

sections.risk_factors.3.quote: Some of the common causes of a penetrating injury include Being hit by a bullet or shrapnel Being hit by a weapon such as a hammer, knife, or baseball bat A head injury that causes a bone fragment to penetrate the skull Some accidents such as explosions, natural disasters, or other extreme events can cause both closed and penetrating TBI in the same person.

sections.signs_symptoms.1.quote: Physical symptoms may include headaches, double or blurred vision, seizure s, convulsions, tremors, nausea and vomiting, slurred speech and/or difficulty swallowing, muscle weakness, paralysis, balance and coordination issues, drainage in the ears or nose, and bowel and/or bladder control issues.

sections.signs_symptoms.2.quote: Slurred speech Weakness or numbness in the arms and legs Loss of coordination Increased confusion, restlessness, or agitation How is traumatic brain injury (TBI) diagnosed?

sections.signs_symptoms.3.quote: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) can be used to assess the patient’s consciousness level.

sections.treatment.3.quote: Surgery to reduce additional damage to your brain, for example to Remove hematomas (clotted blood) Get rid of damaged or dead brain tissue Repair skull fractures Relieve pressure in the skull

sections.complications.2.quote: Cognitive and behavioral symptoms may include lack of consciousness, coma, disorientation and confusion, concentration issues, loss of memory, difficulty thinking, short attention span, mood changes, irritability, frustration, loss of inhibitions, and sleep disorders.

sections.nursing_care.1.quote: Nurses should help patients prepare for surgery and provide care after surgery, such as dressing patients’ wound(s), maintaining oxygenation, positioning the patient, monitoring ICP, and assessing with GCS.

sections.nursing_care.2.quote: Monitor and maintain fluid and electrolyte balance.

sections.patient_teaching.0.quote: Avoiding or minimizing bowel straining, coughing, or bearing down will reduce the risk of increases in ICP.
